text.p: - The major government shake-up which could be announced today is masterminded by the president's chief-of-staff, Anatoly Chubais, who is likely to take a key economic position in the reshuffled cabinet.
- Law-obidient citizens who intend to pay taxes are to go through a complicated bureaucratic procedure of submitting a tax declaration.

- Whatever government reshuffles are be announced today in Russia, ordinary citizens will not be able to feel real changes immediately, so the social tension and opposition activity will be growing for the next few months.
- Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, facing a tough economic and political situation in his country, is expected to make a plea for closer ties with Russia during his coming visit to Moscow.
- After President Yeltsin's address to parliament, Russia's economic and political life will develop according to its inner logic which is usually qhite different from the President's intentions.
- Boris Yeltsin's address to parliament will put an end to the "times of trouble" in Russia when the President was ill and both legislative and executive powers were passive.
- While the Kremlin was busy endlessly rewriting president's address, thousands of angry Russians were sending letters to Boris Yeltsin urging him to step down.
- The powerful anti-NATO sentiment dominant in Russia now is being cultivated to distract public attention from internal problems, says Russia's former Foreign Minister Andrei Kozyrev.
